title: Who pays for tariffs? Insights from recent research
gist: Reviewing the 2026 empirical literature, PIIE economists conclude US consumers and firms bore roughly 90 percent of the burden of Trump's 2025 tariffs, with one study attributing all post-pandemic excess inflation to tariffs and another putting the cumulative CPI effect at ~0.8 percentage points by early 2026. They argue the 'optimal tariff' is a mirage: input-cost and lost-scale-economy channels mean exporters and importers together can absorb more than 100 percent of the tariff, while the legal basis for the tariffs keeps collapsing in court.

themes.theme: Tariff incidence lands on US buyers

insights.claim: Recent studies (Amiti et al. 2026, Fajgelbaum and Khandelwal 2026, Gopinath and Neiman 2025) imply US consumers and firms together bore about 90 percent of the burden of the 2025 US tariffs, not foreign exporters.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The 'foreigners pay' framing is not supported by the data; model tariff costs as a domestic margin and consumer-price hit for US importers and retailers, not as a foreign-exporter subsidy.
insights.quote: US buyers of imports—US consumers and firms together—bore about 90 percent of the tariff burden in 2025
insights.locator: Amiti et al. (2026), Fajgelbaum and Khandelwal

insights.claim: Study after study of the 2018-19 US tariffs found nearly complete pass-through to US buyers of imports, establishing a strong prior that new tariff rounds are borne domestically.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The historical base rate for tariff incidence is domestic; use near-full pass-through as the default assumption when forecasting margin and CPI effects of new tariff announcements.
insights.quote: US buyers of imports suffered essentially the entire burden of the tariffs, with nearly complete pass-through shown in the data.
insights.locator: Still, study after study of the 2018-19

insights.claim: Minton, Ray, and Somale (2026) find tariff pass-through to US consumer prices is complete roughly seven months after implementation with 1-to-1 price effects, and attribute the entirety of post-pandemic excess inflation to tariffs.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: If tariffs explain all excess inflation, tariff removal is a disinflationary lever that would reshape the Fed's rate path; watch tariff rollback headlines as inflation-trade catalysts.
insights.quote: The authors find that tariffs account for the entirety of post-pandemic excess inflation (relative to pre-pandemic inflation).
insights.locator: One recent study (Minton, Ray, and Somale 2026

insights.claim: Cavallo, Llamas, and Vasquez (2026) measure a cumulative tariff effect on the US consumer price index of about 0.8 percentage points by early 2026, with pass-through still incomplete six months after implementation.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: A concrete ~0.8pp CPI wedge gives a size for the tariff inflation impulse and implies further pass-through still in the pipeline if the tariffs persist.
insights.quote: with a cumulative effect on the consumer price index (CPI) of about 0.8 percentage points by early 2026

insights.claim: The eagerness of foreign governments to negotiate under US tariff threats is itself evidence that foreign exporters cannot costlessly redirect exports elsewhere, so tariffs do inflict real pain abroad even while US buyers pay most of the bill.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Both sides lose: exporter margins compress and US buyers pay, so tariff escalation is negative for global trade-exposed equities on both ends of the corridor.
insights.quote: If foreign export firms could easily redirect exports to other partners without cutting prices, their governments could simply ignore US tariff threats without much consequence.
insights.locator: Do foreigners pay for tariffs?

insights.claim: PIIE argues removing tariffs is the fastest available policy answer to US affordability and grocery-price complaints, unlike housing, healthcare, and education costs which need sustained structural reform.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Affordability politics create a live policy option on tariff repeal; consumer-staples and retail importers are the immediate beneficiaries if the political calculus flips.
insights.quote: If policymakers desire a quick and easy response to affordability concerns, removing the tariffs would be an obvious answer.
insights.locator: Thus, the preponderance of evidence indicates

insights.claim: Legal and policy uncertainty around US tariffs makes firms accept compressed margins rather than raise prices they may have to reverse, delaying the inflation impulse rather than removing it.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Near-term corporate margins absorb the hit while the CPI print looks benign; expect a delayed earnings squeeze followed by a delayed consumer-price catch-up.
insights.quote: In the face of policy uncertainty, firms may be more willing to suffer reduced margins in the short run to avoid price increases that they might have to reverse later.
insights.locator: But tariffs take time to affect consumer prices.

insights.claim: Survey evidence cited by PIIE shows US firms are still planning price increases in response to tariffs imposed some time ago, meaning additional pass-through is queued even for tariffs already in force.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Forward inflation risk is embedded in already-announced tariffs; do not treat a stable current CPI as evidence the tariff shock has been absorbed.
insights.quote: Indeed survey evidence(link is external) suggests that firms are still planning price increases in response to tariffs that were imposed some time ago.
insights.locator: They may pause price increases while lobbying

insights.claim: Firms respond to tariffs by lobbying for exemptions and searching for cheaper foreign suppliers (Leibovici and Chinagorom-Abiakalam 2026), which are real business costs of the tariff regime beyond the tariff itself.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The true corporate cost of tariffs exceeds the duty line item; supplier-switching and lobbying overhead erode margins invisibly in SG&A and COGS.
insights.locator: They may pause price increases while lobbying

insights.claim: Bai, Jaccard, and Stumpner (2026) show scanner data from the 2018-19 China tariffs featured full pass-through alongside a product-replacement channel where old barcodes were swapped for new products with higher price-per-weight ratios, i.e. shrinkflation.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Headline shelf-price indices understate tariff pass-through because the cost shows up as smaller pack sizes; measured CPI may be flattering the real consumer hit.
insights.quote: old products were replaced by new products (with different bar codes) that had higher price/weight ratios ("shrinkflation")
insights.locator: Notes 2. Bai, Jaccard, and Stumpner (2026)

insights.claim: Ahn, Rotunno, and Ruta (2026) find US importers bear the full burden of paying tariffs and that the quality of US imports has declined, an adjustment channel that shows up as degraded goods rather than higher measured prices.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Quality downgrading is an unmeasured welfare cost; real consumption is worse than nominal price indices suggest, another reason inflation stats understate tariff damage.
insights.quote: It also finds that the quality of US imports has declined

insights.claim: Tariffs on imported inputs undermine US exporters' competitiveness because US manufacturers pay more for the same inputs than foreign rivals, an effect the Trump administration implicitly concedes by exempting select firms and industries including AI.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Exemption status is a material competitive variable: AI-linked hardware supply chains get relief while unexempted manufacturers eat the input-cost gap.
insights.quote: Even the Trump administration recognizes this dynamic, which is why it has exempted some key firms and industries (including AI) from tariffs on inputs.
insights.locator: Effect on intermediate business costs

insights.claim: Steel and aluminum tariffs remain in force for unexempted manufacturers and the resulting blue-collar employment picture has been disappointing at best, undercutting the manufacturing-jobs rationale for tariffs.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Tariffs have not delivered the promised industrial-jobs dividend; metal-consuming manufacturers remain a cost-squeezed short candidate versus protected metal producers.
insights.quote: the overall jobs picture for blue collar employment has been disappointing at best
insights.locator: Yet other manufacturing firms are less lucky

insights.claim: JPMorganChase (2026) analysis cited by PIIE finds midsize firms may be bearing an especially significant cost from tariffs, indicating the burden is concentrated below the large-cap tier.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Tariff pain is a small- and mid-cap credit and margin story more than a mega-cap one; screen middle-market exposure in private credit and regional bank books.
insights.quote: midsize firms may be bearing an especially significant cost from tariffs
insights.locator: Recent analysis from JPMorganChase (2026)

insights.claim: den Besten et al. (2026) find that tariffs have tended to have contractionary macroeconomic effects throughout history, with the intermediate-input cost channel one mechanism.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Historical evidence frames tariffs as a demand-negative supply shock, arguing for lower growth alongside higher prices rather than a reflationary boom.
insights.quote: tariffs have tended to have contractionary macroeconomic effects throughout history
insights.locator: The intermediate-input cost channel is also negative

insights.claim: Stephen Miran, former chair of Trump's Council of Economic Advisers, claimed in June 2026 that OBBBA's more generous investment deduction provisions could offset higher tariff costs on imported intermediate inputs for US firms.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: This is the administration's official defense against corporate tariff-cost complaints; expect it in policy messaging even though the economics do not hold.
insights.locator: In June 2026, Stephen Miran

insights.claim: Deductibility cannot neutralize a cost increase because firms still pay the after-tax cost of inputs, a point PIIE illustrates by noting the same logic would imply a $25 minimum wage is costless since wages are deductible.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Discount any earnings model that treats OBBBA expensing as neutralizing tariff COGS inflation; the after-tax cost hit to margins is real.
insights.quote: Miran's logic implies that a $25 minimum wage wouldn't be a problem for firms either, since wage costs are deductible.
insights.locator: Any business knows this contention is far from a solution

insights.claim: Higher deficits and debt from OBBBA imply higher interest rates that crowd out domestic investment, compounding rather than offsetting the tariff drag on business.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Fiscal expansion plus tariffs is a double hit to capex: watch long-end yields as the transmission channel from OBBBA to investment-sensitive sectors.
insights.quote: the higher deficits/debt from OBBBA imply higher interest rates, which crowd out domestic investment

themes.theme: Legal fragility of the tariff regime

insights.claim: The Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA-based 'Liberation Day' tariffs unlawful in February 2026, and the US International Trade Court ruled the replacement Section 122 tariffs unlawful in May 2026, with that case on appeal to the federal circuit and unresolved before the Section 122 expiration date of July 24, 2026.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The tariff regime is a serial legal loser being rebuilt under new statutes; refund and repeal scenarios are live tail risks for importers' cost structures.
insights.quote: The Supreme Court ruled the tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) unlawful in February 2026
insights.locator: Notes 4. The Supreme Court ruled the tariffs

insights.claim: The administration's expanded use of Section 301 to recreate the invalidated IEEPA tariff regime is itself vulnerable to legal challenge, and it has invoked Section 338 of the 1930 Smoot-Hawley law to justify new tariffs on Canada.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Each statutory workaround carries fresh litigation risk, keeping trade-policy uncertainty elevated and delaying corporate pricing and sourcing decisions.
insights.quote: To justify new tariffs on Canada, the administration has invoked Section 338
insights.locator: Notes 4. The expanded use of Section 301

insights.claim: A near-constant stream of new US trade policy announcements continues to roil business decisions, making policy volatility itself a distinct cost channel separate from the tariff rate.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Uncertainty suppresses capex and sourcing commitments even where tariff rates are modest; treat announcement cadence as a leading indicator of investment deferral.
insights.locator: There is substantial legal and policy uncertainty

themes.theme: Lost scale economies and the optimal-tariff mirage

insights.claim: Ganapati and Hottman (2026) show tariffs shrink import order sizes and destroy scale economies, so exporters and importers combined can bear burdens totaling more than 100 percent of the tariff's size.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Tariff incidence is not a zero-sum split of the duty; total private-sector cost exceeds revenue collected, so fiscal gains materially understate economic damage.
insights.quote: both parties can together face burdens that total more than 100 percent of the size of the tariff
insights.locator: Forgone scale economies—which normally lower costs

insights.claim: PIIE concludes the 'optimal tariff' is a mirage useful only as a classroom exercise, and that the postwar trade system was designed precisely to stop countries from pursuing it.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The intellectual case for terms-of-trade tariffs is being rejected by mainstream trade economists, weakening the durability of the policy once political winds shift.
insights.quote: The "optimal tariff" is a mirage, useful as a classroom exercise but with little practical relevance.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: Tariffs create opportunities for corruption and rent-seeking, including lobbying for exemptions or for new tariffs on competitors, shifting resources away from optimal uses.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Political access becomes a source of corporate alpha under a tariff regime; exemption-winning firms gain a durable cost advantage unrelated to operating skill.
insights.quote: Tariffs also present opportunities for corruption and rent-seeking
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: Removing tariffs on construction materials would be significant for the US building industry, a targeted channel through which tariff repeal would ease housing costs.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Homebuilders and construction-materials importers are a specific beneficiary basket in any tariff-rollback scenario tied to affordability politics.
insights.quote: But removing tariffs on construction materials would be significant for the building industry.
